idiom_name: interface declaration (explicit implementation, default interface members)
implementation_notes: The interface keyword is this pattern: a named contract that classes, records and structs must implement, and that cannot hold instance state - constants and static members are allowed, fields are not, and interface properties are declarations whose storage lives in the implementing type. Explicit implementation (void IFoo.M()) lets one class satisfy two contracts that declare the same member and keeps the contract member off the class surface, while default interface members (C# 8) give a published contract an implementation so it can gain members without breaking existing implementors - the mechanism that makes interface evolution practical on .NET. An abstract class is still the right tool when the contract needs shared state or a constructor, which an interface can never provide.
pitfalls: An explicitly implemented member is invisible on the concrete type: the call does not compile on a class-typed reference and the member is reachable only through an interface-typed one, which surprises callers who hold the concrete type.

A default interface member is reached through the interface; code bound to the implementing class sees the class's own member or nothing, so adding a default member can change which implementation resolves.
Adding an abstract member to a published interface still breaks every implementor - default members are the escape hatch, and they bring their own most-specific-implementation rules.
A struct used through the interface is boxed, and mutations made on the boxed copy are lost.
